title: The lote tree of the boundary
word: The lote tree of the boundary
hook: he saw Jibril at the lote tree of the utmost boundary, near the garden (53:13–15)

segments.voice: Yesterday, not from desire, and your line was the same: not from desire. Where did you give advice that served them more than you? Day five hundred ninety-nine.

Sidr is a thorny tree of the Arabian desert, the lote tree: small leaves, small fruit, and shade in a hard place. In a hadith in Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad ﷺ tells the women washing his daughter's body to use water and sidr, a practice that continues at funerals today. An ordinary desert tree. And the Qur'an puts one at the edge of everything, at a boundary commentators describe as the farthest point anything created can reach.
screen: `WATER AND SIDR FOR WASHING THE DEAD.`

segments.voice: Surah An-Najm describes two times the Prophet saw the angel Jibril in his true form. The first was on the horizon, near the beginning. The second, in Pickthall's translation: "And verily he saw him yet another time By the lote-tree of the utmost boundary, Nigh unto which is the Garden of Abode." Sidrat al-muntaha. Muntaha means the end point, the furthest limit. Commentators explain it as the place beyond which no created being passes, where the knowledge of creatures stops. Commentators link this second sighting to the Night Journey and Ascension, the Isra' and Mi'raj, when the Prophet was taken through the heavens. 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud both said, in reports in the two Sahihs, that what he saw at the tree was Jibril, as he truly is; Ibn Mas'ud reported six hundred wings. The hadith of the Ascension in Bukhari describes the tree itself: fruits like great clay jars, leaves like elephants' ears, and rivers flowing from its roots. Then the surah says something covered the tree, a covering it doesn't name, and the commentators say it was beyond description. And then a short line: the sight did not swerve, nor did it go beyond. At the edge of everything, he didn't look away, and he didn't grab for more than he was shown. Notice the choice of image. Not a palace or a throne at the boundary, but a tree, the kind that gives shade in hard places. The farthest point of creation is marked by something familiar.
screen: `JIBRIL, SEEN A SECOND TIME.` · `SIDRAT AL-MUNTAHA: THE FARTHEST LIMIT.` · `FRUIT LIKE JARS, LEAVES LIKE EARS.` · `THE SIGHT DID NOT SWERVE.`

segments.voice: The practice: sit at a boundary. If you can, go to an edge: a doorstep, a window, the shore, the end of a street where the fields begin. If you can't, picture one. Sit with one foot on each side, inside and out, here and beyond. Notice the line. Then do what the verse describes: look steadily, without swerving, and without reaching for more than what's in front of you. If you pray, you can ask for that steadiness. The bell holds the time.
The lote tree of the boundary. Sidrat al-muntaha: the tree at the farthest limit of creation, where the Prophet saw Jibril a second time. Today's word.
screen: `THE LOTE TREE OF THE BOUNDARY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the farthest tree. Today, when you pass a tree, let it remind you that the edge of everything is marked by something that gives shade. Day five hundred ninety-nine.

howItsDone: Muslims remember the Isra' and Mi'raj, some with a yearly observance in the month of Rajab, retelling the journey to the lote tree and the gift of the five daily prayers; sidr leaves are still used in many places for washing the dead.

fork.reveal: 53:17: steady, without looking away and without overreaching.

original.note: Arabic: the lote tree of the utmost boundary (53:14).

trapdoor: what you thought: a magical tree in paradise.
what it means: a lote tree at the farthest limit of creation, where the Prophet saw Jibril in his true form.
what a scholar hears: muntaha, the end point, explained as where creatures' knowledge stops; Bukhari's Ascension hadith describes jar-like fruit and rivers from its roots.

notes: Pickthall wording of 53:13–15 quoted from memory; please confirm.
Hadith numbers cited from memory; confirm.
Commemorating the Isra' and Mi'raj on 27 Rajab is widespread but its date and observance are debated among scholars; howItsDone says 'often'.
Some early views held the Prophet saw his Lord (attributed to Ibn 'Abbas); the script follows 'A'ishah and Ibn Mas'ud on Jibril. A Keeper may wish to note the difference.
